title: Can Lesson Observations Be Developmental and Evaluative?
author: Nick Nickhart
summary: Drawing on Lee Shulman's concept of 'signature pedagogies,' Nick Nickhart argues that lesson observation in teaching suffers from a persistent blurring of two distinct purposes — developmental coaching and evaluative judgement — because both share the identical surface feature of someone watching and giving feedback. He walks through the teacher's perspective (where implicit distrust means observations are read as evaluative even when framed as developmental) and the observer's perspective (where Dunning-Kruger-style overconfidence leads many observers to believe they can diagnose next steps and judge quality in the same visit), concluding that genuine separation of purpose is achievable but requires deliberate structural design rather than good intentions alone. His proposed conditions differ sharply by purpose: developmental observation needs subject-specialist observers and sustained trusting relationships, while evaluative observation needs calibrated criteria, trained observers, multiple raters, and triangulation with other evidence. The piece ends by cautioning that structural separation is necessary but not sufficient — the implicit, culturally read value system around observation only shifts once teachers experience developmental feedback as genuinely useful and evaluative judgements as fair.
points: Applies Shulman's 'signature pedagogies' framework to argue that lesson observation's problem is not method but purpose-blurring: the same surface act (someone watching and giving feedback) is used for both developmental coaching and evaluative judgement.

Argues that merely rebranding observation as 'developmental' (e.g., dropping individual lesson grading) does not resolve the underlying validity problem, and may even worsen it, since developmental observation demands more contextual and subject expertise than evaluative observation.
Uses the Dunning-Kruger effect to explain why many observers overestimate their ability to both diagnose a teacher's next developmental step and fairly judge teaching quality within the same visit.

Specifies different structural conditions for each purpose: developmental observation requires subject-specialist observers and sustained trust; evaluative observation requires calibrated criteria, trained observers, multiple independent raters, and triangulation with other evidence.

Concludes that structural separation of developmental and evaluative observation is necessary but not sufficient — the teacher's implicit, culturally-read sense of what observation is 'really' for only shifts once both purposes are experienced as genuinely useful and genuinely fair.
quotes: One of Lee Shulman's contributions to educational theory is the idea of signature pedagogies: different professions have different ways of training the next generation.

From a school leader perspective, two important things (teacher development and evaluation of teaching quality) can often be driven by what looks on the surface to be the same thing: someone watching and giving feedback.

My guess is that shifting to a more developmental model of lessons observation further compounds the reliability and validity issues that we know exist. Developmental observation requires even more contextual and subject knowledge than evaluative observation.
They might say they're here to help me develop but I know I'm still being judged. Whatever they say is the purpose, the real reason is evaluating my teaching.

The conditions under which a teacher might genuinely experience both developmental and evaluative observation positively are knowable: high trust, transparent purpose, a sustained relationship with the observer, and a clear separation between the developmental conversation and any evaluative record.
The Dunning-Kruger effect describes how limited knowledge in a domain produces overestimated competence and lesson observation is no exception.

It changes when developmental observations produce something teachers find genuinely useful, when evaluative observations are conducted with sufficient rigour that their conclusions feel fair and when teachers can reliably tell the difference between the two.
